questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
P: Good mobile phones are not cheap
Q: Cheap mobile phones are not good

L: P implies Q
M: Q implies P
N: P is equivalent to Q
Which one of the following about L, M, and N is CORRECT?

options.D: L, M and N are TRUE.

questions.explanation:
Let G = good, C = cheap.
- P: [latex]G\rightarrow\neg C[/latex]
- Q: [latex]C\rightarrow\neg G[/latex]

Q is the contrapositive of P, so P [latex]\equiv[/latex] Q. Hence P implies Q, Q implies P, and P is equivalent to Q.

Answer: L, M and N are TRUE

questions.question: Let x and Y be finite sets and f:x[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]Y be a function. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

options.A: For any subsets A and B of x, |f(A[latex]\cup[/latex]B)|=|f(A)|+|f(B)|
options.B: For any subsets A and B of x, f(A[latex]\cap[/latex]B) =f(A)[latex]\cap[/latex]f(B)
options.C: For any subsets A and B of x, |f(A[latex]\cap[/latex]B)| = min{|f (A)| ,|f(B)|}
options.D: For any subsets S and T of Y, [latex]f^{-1}(S\cap T)=f^{-1}(S)\cap f^{-1}(T)[/latex]

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Option 1 fails when f(A) and f(B) overlap.
- Option 2 fails for non-injective f: A = {1}, B = {2}, f(1) = f(2) = y gives [latex]f(A\cap B)=\emptyset[/latex] but [latex]f(A)\cap f(B)=\{y\}[/latex].
- Option 3 fails for the same example.
- Option 4: [latex]x\in f^{-1}(S\cap T)\iff f(x)\in S[/latex] and [latex]f(x)\in T\iff x\in f^{-1}(S)\cap f^{-1}(T)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] always true.

Answer: [latex]f^{-1}(S\cap T)=f^{-1}(S)\cap f^{-1}(T)[/latex]

questions.question:
Which one of the following statements is TRUE about every n x n matrix with only real
eigenvalues?

options.A: If the trace of the matrix is positive and the determinant of the matrix is negative, at least one of its eigenvalues is negative.
options.B: If the trace of the matrix is positive, all its eigenvalues are positive.
options.C: If the determinant of the matrix is positive, all its eigenvalues are positive.
options.D: If the product of the trace and determinant of the matrix is positive, all its eigenvalues are positive.

questions.explanation:
Trace = sum of eigenvalues, determinant = product of eigenvalues.

- If det [latex]\lt[/latex] 0, the product is negative, so at least one eigenvalue is negative [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] option 1 true.
- Counter-examples for others: eigenvalues 3, [latex]-[/latex]1 (trace [latex]\gt[/latex] 0); [latex]-[/latex]1, [latex]-[/latex]2 (det [latex]\gt[/latex] 0); [latex]-[/latex]1, [latex]-[/latex]1, 5 (trace and det both positive).

Answer: If trace is positive and determinant is negative, at least one eigenvalue is negative

Consider the following processors (ns stands for nanoseconds). Assume that the pipeline registers have zero latency.
P1: Four-stage pipeline with stage latencies 1 ns, 2 ns, 2 ns, 1 ns.
P2: Four-stage pipeline with stage latencies 1 ns, 1.5 ns, 1.5 ns, 1.5 ns.
P3: Five-stage pipeline with stage latencies 0.5 ns, 1 ns, 1 ns, 0.6 ns, 1 ns.
P4: Five-stage pipeline with stage latencies 0.5 ns, 0.5 ns, 1 ns, 1 ns, 1.1 ns.

Clock period = largest stage latency.

- P3: 1 ns [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1 GHz

questions.question: Suppose depth first search is executed on the graph below starting at some unknown vertex. Assume that a recursive call to visit a vertex is made only after first checking that the vertex has not been visited earlier. Then the maximum possible recursion depth (including the initial call) is _________.
questions.explanation:
Max recursion depth = number of vertices on the longest simple path DFS can follow.

- Left 3 [latex]\times[/latex] 3 grid: a snake path covers all 9 vertices, ending at its bottom-right corner.
- Bottom middle vertex: 1 (its pendant above is a dead end, so skip it).
- Right 3 [latex]\times[/latex] 3 grid: enter at the bottom-left corner; we must end at the middle-right vertex to reach the pendant. A grid is bipartite (5 corner-coloured, 4 other), so a corner-to-middle path can cover only 8 vertices.
- Right pendant: 1

Depth = 9 + 1 + 8 + 1 = 19

Answer: 19

Consider the decision problem 2CNFSAT defined as follows:
{ [latex]\phi[/latex] | [latex]\phi[/latex] is a satisfiable propositional formula in CNF with at most two literal per clause}
For example, [latex]\phi =(x_{1} \vee x_{2}) \wedge (x_{1} \vee \bar{x_{3}}) \wedge (x_{2} \vee x_{4})[/latex] is a Boolean formula and it is in 2CNFSAT.

So 2-SAT is solved in polynomial (linear) time by graph reachability.

Answer: solvable in polynomial time by reduction to directed graph reachability

questions.question: An instruction pipeline has five stages, namely, instruction fetch (IF), instruction decode and register fetch (ID/RF), instruction execution (Ex), memory access (MEM), and register write back (WB) with stage latencies 1 ns, 2.2 ns, 2 ns, 1 ns, and 0.75 ns, respectively (ns stands for nanoseconds). To gain in terms of frequency, the designers have decided to split the ID/RF stage into three stages (ID, RF1, RF2) each of latency 2.2/3 ns. Also, the Ex stage is split into two stages (Ex1, Ex2) each of latency 1 ns. The new design has a total of eight pipeline stages. A program has 20% branch instructions which execute in the Ex stage and produce the next instruction pointer at the end of the Ex stage in the old design and at the end of the Ex2 stage in the new design. The IF stage stalls after fetching a branch instruction until the next instruction pointer is computed. All instructions other than the branch instruction have an average CPI of one in both the designs. The execution times of this program on the old and the new design are P and Q nanoseconds, respectively. The value of P/Q is __________
questions.explanation:
Old design: clock = 2.2 ns. Branch resolved at end of stage 3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 stall cycles.
CPI = 0.8 [latex]\times[/latex] 1 + 0.2 [latex]\times[/latex] 3 = 1.4 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P = 1.4 [latex]\times[/latex] 2.2 = 3.08 ns per instruction

New design: clock = 1 ns. Branch resolved at end of Ex2 = stage 6 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 5 stall cycles.
CPI = 0.8 [latex]\times[/latex] 1 + 0.2 [latex]\times[/latex] 6 = 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q = 2 ns per instruction

P/Q = 3.08 / 2 = 1.54

Answer: 1.54

questions.question:

nanoseconds for a read operation with a miss in cache, 2 nanoseconds for a write operation
with a hit in cache and 10 nanoseconds for a write operation with a miss in cache. Execution
of a sequence of instructions involves 100 instruction fetch operations, 60 memory operand
read operations and 40 memory operand write operations. The cache hit-ratio is 0.9. The
average memory access time (in nanoseconds) in executing the sequence of instructions is

Reads = 100 fetches + 60 operands = 160, writes = 40.

- Avg write = 0.9 [latex]\times[/latex] 2 + 0.1 [latex]\times[/latex] 10 = 2.8 ns

Average = [latex]\frac{160\times1.4+40\times2.8}{200}=\frac{224+112}{200}=1.68[/latex]

Answer: 1.68

questions.question:
There are two elements x,y in a group (G,*) such that every element in the group can be written as a product of some number of x's and y's in some order. It is known that
x * x = y * y = x * y *x * y = y* x * y *x = e

 WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT custId
